items.title: Japanese Indie Gaming Publishers Are Doing Things Differently
items.author: Alicia Haddick
items.summary: Tokyo Game Show 2026 was light on major upcoming releases, in part due to a quieter-than-normal fall for gaming outside of the unavoidable spectre of Grand
items.text:
Tokyo Game Show 2026 was light on major upcoming releases, in part due to a quieter-than-normal fall for gaming outside of the unavoidable spectre of Grand Theft Auto VI. That being said, there were still things to see at this year’s event—you just had to know where to look. Take a glance at the world of Japanese indie gaming showcased on the convention floor, for example, and you would find a wonderful assortment of unique experiences rooted in Japanese social issues and experiences, the results of a notable divergence from how Japanese indie games have historically been developed, supported, and shared with players.

It may be somewhat surprising that it’s taken until the last few years for a groundswell of Japanese indie developers to establish themselves within the domestic games industry. Indie gaming has thrived since the late 2000s outside of Japan thanks to digital storefronts on consoles, and Japan itself is host to events like Comiket, where both amateur original and derivative works in various art forms, including video games, can be sold. These works are known as doujin.

At their core, doujin games were acts of love created by hobbyist developers to sell to core fans, whether original or derivative of another IP. The Touhou franchise, arguably the biggest example of Japanese independent gaming media in the past 30 years, rose from this subculture. Otherwise, however, doujin has been mostly a passion-fueled endeavor, a way to share creations with like-minded fans more than a path to profit or a potential career.

Yet as global indie darlings like Undertale, sustained marketing efforts like Nintendo’s Indie World, and Japanese indie companies like Q-Games and Orbitals developer Shapefarm find success, some have felt encouraged to break from the norm of major company employment and challenge themselves to give indie game development a shot. With more teams and creators embracing this field, the results are often unique experiences that channel Japanese societal practices and personal experiences.

Mask It, featured at Tokyo Game Show this year as part of the Selected Indie 80, a program designed to bring attention to standout indie efforts, began as a Game Jam project during this year’s Global Game Jam. Players assume the role of a news editor whose job is to make the everyday news more “exciting” to hit targets and please editors, often by deliberately blurring over photographs or making other edits in stories as you seek sensationalistic virality. These tweaks could merely be done for comedic effect, or to insinuate sinister implications and have a corrosive impact on public discourse or opinion, making the game a reflection of increasing concerns in Japan over the spread of false information on social media and by politicians, alongside concerns about AI.

Timemoon, from developer Kenkou Land, is a narrative adventure in which you play as Clark, a taxi driver in the near future taking passengers in his time-traveling taxi. A passenger’s destination may not just be a location but a moment in time, and following the mysterious death of the president, your chauffeuring of high-profile passengers may be key to understanding the possible use of time travel in their murder.

Then you have Late Fee Girls, an RPG following three girls who run a video store and make secondary revenue as Exorcist Streamers, going out to fight ghosts from haunted videotapes. It’s an ambitious project for solo developer Urimo, who is concurrently selling doujin comics that contain character sketches and in-universe commentary from the characters as development continues.

There were plenty of other exciting indie games at TGS this year, too, like Tanuki: Pon’s Summer, which features a bicycling tanuki running errands and pulling tricks like Tony Hawk, and Iron Bramble, a Metroidvania with a unique grappling hook–driven movement system. But it’s the doujin magazines of Late Fee Girls that reveal, on a more intimate scale, how Japanese doujin and indie game creators are finding different pathways toward funding development, building audiences, and sustaining their work.

Developers like them are increasingly embracing the ecosystems in place for small creators to sell their creations and showcase their work at everything from vast conventions to minor art gallery spaces as a way to fund game development. Selling stickers or postcards or a small zine of concept art may not make a huge dent in development budgets, but it helps by also leaving the people who buy them invested in the game as they wait for the release and spread the word.

And these events, even those that aren’t gaming-specific, can draw thousands of eyes to your game. Some will sell doujins even at more generalized events like Comitia, whose quarterly Tokyo events attract over 30,000 attendees each, while Comiket can attract over 300,000 people over its two days.

This strategy of selling merchandise for in-development and post-release games while also looking toward multimedia expansion to make an impression and grow an IP’s audience was the founding principle of a number of Japan-centric publishers showcasing at this year’s TGS.

The winner of the best indie game at Tokyo Game Show, taking away the Platinum Prize for best game as part of the event’s Selected Indie 80, was Finding Polka, a beautiful game about searching for a missing dog in a dense town, with a visual style defined by hand-drawn sketches for every character and animation. Also taking away top prizes at Gamescom and Japanese indie gaming event Bitsummit, the game is published by Parco Games worldwide, a new games publisher founded by the Japanese department store chain of the same name.

The company’s large department stores across Japan are home to far more than just clothing, with Parco investing heavily in everything from art exhibitions to stage plays. Parco Games is also forming partnerships outside of publishing, like a pop-up store for Kojima Productions, and its efforts with indie developers extend to merchandising.

Thus, you can buy Finding Polka t-shirts from Parco, sold alongside major fashion brands online, and the company is embracing an arts-driven approach to the games it partners with. Finding Polka is one of the first titles it’s publishing globally, but the company is also working with Turkish team Error Thing to publish Deperson worldwide, a highlight of the show for its unnerving creativity. This psychedelic horror game set inside a mental hospital features alluring hand-drawn art as you speak with other patients, learning about their conditions and dealing with amnesia. While not a Japanese game, Parco’s interest in artistic expression made partnering with it a natural fit, according to the Parco Games team.

“We aren’t a game-centric company, but we have a long history of discovering new talent and innovative forms of expression, and bringing their appeal to a wide audience,” explains Yudai Kawamura from Parco Games. “We believe our experience here can be applied to the world of gaming as well. Parco has physical spaces where people can gather such as stores, event spaces, galleries and theaters, and allowing people to experience games not just by selling them but through exhibitions and events is something unique to what we offer.”

The company’s hope is that emphasizing a game as a long-term piece of art beyond just the video-game space will help it to resonate. And this approach doesn’t stop with Parco Games. In recent years, Shueisha Games has used its parent company’s experience as a manga publisher to assist in expanding its successful games into new mediums like novels and pop-up merchandising stores in physical retail locations.

Beyond simply being great games by a breadth of developers from a range of backgrounds, these games all feature original ideas and are being supported by publishers for whom gaming is just one avenue to promote the developers they work with. It elevates games to the level of an exhibition in an art gallery, and a conversation piece that can linger beyond the next refresh of a digital storefront, creating an environment in which it’s easier to take a risk on a new idea.

Currently, the Japanese indie games able to break out internationally are viral phenomena like Meccha Chamelion and Exit 8, but it’s titles like Finding Polka that showcase a creative indie scene that can sustain itself, and that invites global players to explore what it holds. Japanese indie gaming was thriving at Tokyo Game Show, because it chose to do things differently.

items.title: “Cupertino” is a Smart Big Tech Procedural
items.author: Jen Chaney
items.summary: Movie theaters are currently inundated with major motion pictures that examine and/or indict the behavior of wealthy Silicon Valley leaders, including Meta’s
items.text:
Movie theaters are currently inundated with major motion pictures that examine and/or indict the behavior of wealthy Silicon Valley leaders, including Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg (“The Social Reckoning”), Theranos fraudster Elizabeth Holmes (“You Can See Everything”), Elon Musk (Alex Gibney’s “Musk”), and OpenAI’s Sam Altman (“Artificial”). Television is in on the trend, too. In November, Netflix will remind us of the implosion of cryptocurrency fund FTX and its founder, Sam Bankman-Fried, in “The Altruists.”

On CBS and Paramount+ starting Thursday, there’s “Cupertino,” a broadcast-network procedural that doesn’t zero in on a real-life tech bro, but does raise a lot of sobering questions about the industry currently attempting to cram A.I. down the throats of the global populace.

Created by Michelle and Robert King—the showrunning power couple responsible for “The Good Wife,” “The Good Fight,” “Evil,” “Elsbeth,” and ensuring that CBS still offers quality programming in primetime—the series is a legal drama about an upstart law firm that focuses specifically on clients who want to sue powerful Silicon Valley companies.

“I’m sick of people controlling my fate, and my guess is there are a lot of people out there that feel the same way but don’t have anyone to represent them,” says Michael Price (Mike Colter of “Luke Cage” and “Evil”), an attorney who co-founded, then got edged out of, an extremely successful big tech company called S-Talk.

He’s explaining his reasons for wanting to start an agency that takes on the cases against Magnificent 7-level companies that other firms are too afraid to touch. But he could just as easily be describing this show’s appeal to an American audience frustrated by the unemployment rate, the disproportionate power and wealth of the billionaire class, and the non-stop insistence that everyone get on board with artificial intelligence.

Unlike the other projects mentioned above, “Cupertino” does not focus on the idiosyncrasies/neuroses of a single, perceived “genius.” It is more general in its depiction of big tech, which enables it to feel both timely and, perhaps, more relatable to the average person.

Pictured (L-R): Rachel Keller as Olivia Siffre and Mike Colter as Michael Price. Photo: Elizabeth Fisher/CBS ©2026 CBS Broadcasting, Inc. All Rights Reserved.

While there are some key storylines that run throughout the first 10 episodes—the rivalry between Michael and his showboating lawyer father (Joe Morton); another, separate rivalry between Michael and his ex, also an attorney (Renée Elise Goldsberry, who co-starred opposite Colter on “Evil”); and, most importantly, an ongoing narrative about a particularly dangerous form of AI—this is largely a case-of-the-week type of show.

With its quick, plot-driven pacing, “Cupertino” is episodic, mainstream network storytelling that shows, like so much of the Kings’ output, that it’s still possible to make smart, sophisticated, digestible television within that framework.

As Michael, Colter is dignified, pragmatic and, if I’m being honest, not wildly different in demeanor from David, the priest the actor played on “Evil.” But he’s a persuasive lead in both shows, so I’m not going to complain too much about any overlap. While Michael believes in justice and the rule of law, he’s not some anti-capitalist hero who wants to burn down all of Silicon Valley. He simply sees a gap in the marketplace that needs filling. “When you’re in the middle of the ocean, you don’t sell people more water,” he explains to Goldsberry’s Nichole. “You sell them life jackets.”

His partner at the new firm, Olivia Siffre (Rachel Keller), a devout Christian and gifted lawyer who also gets fired from S-Talk after being sexually harassed by the head of the company, is the bleeding heart in this pairing. Keller and Colter have an organic, friendly chemistry that, to the show’s credit, is supportive without being romantic, at least not in these early episodes.

But the standout performances in “Cupertino” come from the two actors who provide the most comedic relief in a drama that doesn’t shy away from poking fun at the always-pitching culture of venture capitalism. Ella Stiller (daughter of Ben Stiller and Christine Taylor) gets a break-out role as Christy Palladino, a third employee who gets fired from S-Talk and becomes the receptionist at Price and Siffre, where she proves to be a fantastic investigator for her attorney bosses.

Christy is particularly adept at tracking down leads and calling in favors from her extensive family of blue-collar workers; after being escorted out of the S-Talk building, she phones her electrician uncle, who proceeds to turn the power on and off in that office and enrage everyone still “lucky” enough to be employed there. Christy knows nothing about technology, but she loves to stick it to the man. Her default expression is resting “you’ve got to be kidding me” face, and Stiller has got that expression down pat.

Pictured (L-R): Ella Stiller as Christy Palladino, Mike Colter as Michael Price, and Rachel Keller as Olivia Siffre. Photo: Elizabeth Fisher/CBS ©2026 CBS Broadcasting, Inc. All Rights Reserved

Then there’s Busy Phillips, who’s cast as Natalia Boutella, a key investor in the new firm who also happens to be divorced from a tech executive played by Fisher Stevens who is not Jeff Bezos, but also is totally Jeff Bezos. Natalia is less interested in sticking it to the man than she is in sticking it to that particular man. When he denies that he has gained weight after she tells him he “got fat,” Natalia counters: “You dined with the president, you had a front row seat to that inauguration, you bought a billion-dollar yacht. You got fat.” Phillips utters lines like that as if they’re coated in venom.

(As an added bonus, every time she and Goldsberry appear in the same scene, it’s like a partial “Girls5Eva” reunion, and that alone deserves a fresh designation on Rotten Tomatoes.)

The Kings and co. tackle numerous zeitgeisty tech trends; one episode focuses on a teenager compelled to kill his father by a chatbot, while another, which happens to debut less than a week before the midterms, zeroes in on prediction websites used to manipulate elections.

But “Cupertino” is not a purely anti-A.I. narrative. The episodes also highlight situations where technological assistance can help. In one, Christy gets incredibly frustrated by an A.I. agent she attempts to train by making sure its knowledge of horror movies is up to snuff. (“In which state did ‘The Blair Witch Project‘ take place?” she asks. “Wisconsin,” the agent cheerfully responds. Christy: “No, Maryland, moron.”) But she’s pretty grateful for that moron when he can warn her not to take a sip of a drink that’s been spiked at a bar.

If “Cupertino” has an official position on technology, it’s that it can be very useful, but it desperately needs significant, legally enforceable guardrails. This is an opinion shared by most sentient beings with anything akin to a conscience. This series dares to suggest that there’s a world where guardrails could be put in place, and where the “little guys” in the tech world have a chance to be heard. Maybe that’s a fantasy, but it’s one that’s extremely entertaining to live in for 42 minutes every week.

Image via Netflix

Published Oct 11, 2026, 6:00 AM EDT

Denis is a news writer for Collider with close to five years of experience in the industry. He has analyzed shows across different genres, formats and styles. His favorite types of articles to write are exciting news updates and episodic deep-dives. He might say he doesn't have a favorite show, but he has watched The Wire, Shameless, The Big Bang Theory, and The Blacklist more than once. Denis is increasingly becoming focused on the global streaming arena and how media connects with audiences in various markets. Find him on X tweeting about something random that occurred to him about a TV show or the industry in general.

For three seasons, Gabriel Basso has embodied Peter Sutherland in Netflix's hit action thriller, The Night Agent. Basso plays a character dragged from obscurity by the FBI and thrust into a massive conspiracy that tests him in ways he never thought possible. The role demands a lot from Basso, both physically, because of the action scenes, and emotionally, given how deeply entangled the conspiracy goes. However, The Night Agent is gearing up for its final run, but before Peter blows open his final conspiracy on Netflix, Basso has his next role lined up, and it hits the screen this week.

This story is a slight departure from The Night Agent, but Basso has played a range of characters throughout his career. This time he puts his romance chops to the test in Prime Video's 106-minute romance drama. Basso plays Charlie in Love of Your Life, a film directed by Rachel Morrison (The Fire Inside) and written by Julia Cox.

Details about Love of Your Life remain scarce, but Margaret Qualley stars as Maya, a young woman whose world is about to be upended after meeting Charlie. Their chance encounter births a sweeping romance that changes Maya's future and forces her to "reckon with who she is, what she wants, and how to love again." The film's description remains cryptic about what that future looks like and how Charlie fits into it. The good news is that Love of Your Life comes to Prime Video this week on Wednesday, October 14, after a limited theatrical release on October 7, so viewers can discover everything for themselves. Other cast members include Aaron Pierre (Lanterns), Patrick Schwarzenegger (The White Lotus), Catherine Keener (Capote), Tamara Lawrance (Kindred), and Corey Johnson (Morbius).

Collider Exclusive · 8 Questions · 2 Minutes
Which Iconic Romance Is Your Favorite?
Harry & Sally · Love & Basketball · Heated Rivalry · Titanic

Four great love stories, and four completely different ideas of what love actually is. One is a friendship that took twelve years to admit itself. One is two people who refuse to stop competing. One happens entirely behind closed doors. And one lasts five days and never stops mattering. Eight questions decide which one is really yours.

🍂Harry & Sally(1989)

🏀Love & Basketball(2000)

🏒Heated Rivalry(HBO Max)

🚢Titanic(1997)

FIND YOUR ROMANCE →

01

How does your love story start?
The first scene tells you what kind of story this is going to be.

AWe are friends for years before either of us says anything.
BWe want the same thing and neither of us backs down.
CNobody can know, including our closest friends.
DOne look across a room and everything changes.

NEXT QUESTION →

02

What do the two of you keep arguing about?
Every great romance has one fight it has over and over.

AWhether this is actually happening, and what to call it.
BWhose career comes first this year.
CWhether we will ever be honest about this in public.
DNothing small. When we fight, it is about everything.

NEXT QUESTION →

03

How do you show somebody that you love them?
Grand gestures are easy to write. This is the harder question.

AI remember every single thing they have told me.
BI show up to the things that matter to them.
CI keep their secrets like they are my own.
DI would give up something enormous for them.

NEXT QUESTION →

04

What is actually standing in the way?
There is always something. Which something tells you the genre.

ATiming. We keep finding each other at the wrong moment.
BAmbition. We both want big lives and they do not match.
CThe world. It is not safe to be open about this yet.
DEverybody around us has decided this cannot happen.

NEXT QUESTION →

05

Which romantic moment gets you every single time?
Be honest. There is one that works on you and you know which.

ASomebody running across a city to say it before midnight.
BSomebody in the stands who stayed until the very end.
CA look across a crowded room that nobody else catches.
DSomebody promising to hold on, and meaning it.

NEXT QUESTION →

06

What would you actually risk for the right person?
Every romance asks this. Most people find out far too late.

AA friendship I could never get back.
BThe plan I have had for my life since I was a kid.
CMy privacy. All of it would become public.
DEverything. I would not think about it for long.

NEXT QUESTION →

07

Where are the two of you in ten years?
Some love stories are about the meeting. Some are about the staying.

AStill talking. We have never run out of things to say.
BBuilding something together, both of us still ambitious.
CFinally open about it, after years of being careful.
DApart, and I still think about it constantly.

NEXT QUESTION →

08

Which of these sounds most like something you would say?
Eight questions in, this is the one that decides your romance.

AI would rather talk to you than anybody else, forever.
BI am not giving up either of us. We find a way to have both.
CThis is mine, and I am not explaining it to anyone.
DI would do the whole thing again, even knowing how it ends.

REVEAL MY ROMANCE →

Roll The Credits
Your Romance Is…

Four love stories, four completely different ideas of what it means to
be somebody's person. This is the one that matches how you actually fall, and what it would ask of
you.

When Harry Met Sally · 1989

Harry & Sally

You do not fall for strangers. You fall for the person you have
already been talking to for years, which is the slowest and by some distance the most
durable way anybody has found to do this.

When Harry Met Sally made the case that the best romance is an argument you enjoy,
conducted over a decade, by two people refusing to admit what is happening.

You want to be known rather than swept away. Somebody who remembers your worst story is
doing better work than anybody arriving with flowers.

The film is unusually honest about timing. These two are wrong for each other repeatedly
until suddenly they are not, and neither of them engineered it.

You would still be talking about everything at eighty. That is the entire promise.

Love & Basketball · 2000

Love & Basketball

You want a partner, not an audience. Somebody who wants their own
life as badly as you want yours, and who would never ask you to be smaller to make the
relationship easier.

This is the rare romance where both people have a real career and the film takes both of
them equally seriously.

You would rather be pushed than protected. The right person for you is also a bit of a
rival, and that never entirely goes away.

It understands the actual problem in ambitious relationships. Not whether you love each
other, but whose turn it is this year.

You would still be competing at forty. That is how you would know it was working.

Heated Rivalry · Rachel Reid · HBO Max 2025

Heated Rivalry

The intensity was never the problem. The secrecy is. You are
drawn to a love that lives entirely in private, and to the particular ache of wanting
somebody you are not supposed to want.

Heated Rivalry runs on the oldest engine in romance: two people on opposite sides,
meeting in secret, getting far more attached than either of them planned.

You keep your private life genuinely private, and something in you finds hidden things
more real than public ones.

The tension is not only between the two of them. It is between what they have and what
it would cost either one to say it out loud.

Years of this, and the whole story is really about whether either of them will finally
stop hiding.

Titanic · 1997

Titanic

You do not do this cautiously. When it happens for you it is
immediate and total and it rearranges everything, and you would not accept a smaller version
of it.

Titanic gave us the biggest romance in film history and then made it last about five
days, which is precisely the point of it.

You measure love by intensity rather than duration. A few days of the real thing beats
decades of something merely comfortable.

The film is not only about the romance. It is about a woman who went on to live an
enormous life afterwards because of it.

You would still be telling this story at a hundred years old, and telling it exactly the
same way.

What Is the Current Status of 'The Night Agent?'

Following three successful seasons, Netflix renewed The Night Agent for a fourth and final season. Production took place in Los Angeles and concluded last month, meaning the season is on track for a 2027 release date. Details about the final season are not out yet, but as usual, a new arc brings new people into Peter's orbit. Viewers can expect to see new faces, including Titus Welliver (Bosch), Trevante Rhodes (Moonlight), Abigail Breslin (Little Miss Sunshine), Annabeth Gish (Midnight Mass), David Denman (Rebel Ridge), Li Jun Li (Sinners), and Elizabeth Lail (You). Additionally, Luciane Buchanan will return for the final season after being absent in the third season.

Watch Basso in Love of Your Life on October 14, before the final season of The Night Agent in 2027. Stay tuned to Collider for more updates.

When Harry Met Sally · 1989

Harry & Sally

You do not fall for strangers. You fall for the person you have
already been talking to for years, which is the slowest and by some distance the most

life as badly as you want yours, and who would never ask you to be smaller to make the
relationship easier.

them equally seriously.
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/love-of-your-life-prime-video-4.jpg?q=49&fit=crop&w=145&h=85&dpr=2

rival, and that never entirely goes away.

It understands the actual problem in ambitious relationships. Not whether you love each
other, but whose turn it is this year.

https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/love-of-your-life-prime-video-1.jpg?q=49&fit=crop&w=145&h=85&dpr=2

The intensity was never the problem. The secrecy is. You are
drawn to a love that lives entirely in private, and to the particular ache of wanting
somebody you are not supposed to want.

meeting in secret, getting far more attached than either of them planned.
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/love-of-your-life-prime-video-1.jpeg?q=49&fit=crop&w=145&h=85&dpr=2

stop hiding.

https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/love-of-your-life-prime-video-3.jpg?q=49&fit=crop&w=145&h=85&dpr=2

You do not do this cautiously. When it happens for you it is
immediate and total and it rearranges everything, and you would not accept a smaller version

items.text:
The descent into autumn continues: this week I slept with an extra blanket on the bed. I'm not into swapping the duvet out for the winter tog yet, I'll be holding off on that until at least December, but the laying of the first blanket is a true marker of autumn's arrival.

Another change I was telling the team about to definitely rapt fascination was that I've brought the dehumidifier out to reduce condensation in the living room when drying washing. Not only that, I'm combining it with the fan I bought in summer to keep the air circulating. Reader, I don't mean to boast, but it dried two loads of washing including heavy ply towels overnight.

But enough about my successes, this is what the rest of the team are up to.

Edwin
This weekend I'll be checking out the demo for Ablahshikar, a turn-based ship-salvaging game with ASCII art and some extremely extra writing. As the developers put it: "Thy wrists y-braced to a wan terminal of bone-whyte and tarnysshed latoun, þou steerest Ablahshikar by murke point-nettes and sputteryng tables." Ta to former RPS scribe and current Steam Hype editor Dominic Tarason for passing it on.

Mark
I've got another mystery game I'm slowly chipping away at. When I'm not on with that I might finally get around to checking out The Witcher 3's new coat of paint. I just need to double check I've not got any residue left over from a previous modded installation where I'd turned Gerry into a man-torsoed and horse-legged centaur, since that might cause the new version of the all-timer RPG to get a bit confused. I'm also due a return to Star Wars: Galactic Racer for a proper taste of its multiplayer now the podracing gates have opened to everyone.

Ollie
This weekend I'll be away from my... well, not my PC, because that's still borked. But my PC setup. Which is an important distinction, because for the time being I've been plugging my two monitors and all my peripherals into my laptop and playing on there, to varying degrees of success. But this weekend I'm travelling, so I've packed up said laptop - and also brought along my Steam Deck, my Steam Frame, and my Steam Controller. No, I'm not sponsored. I just don't know what I want to play or how I want to play it.

James
Wait, Ollie has a Steam Frame? At last, a second person I know who does. On a related note, there's a Titanfall 2 VR mod I've been meaning to try, and am finally free enough from review duties to make the time for it.

Jeremy
I'm playing an upcoming game that involves exploring a very large area, attacking things, and occasionally eating big pieces of chicken. You commentators who have been following my WAPs recently will figure it out.

Callum
Upon learning it was his one year anniversary at RPS, Callum announced he was departing for the sewers to "make good on the pact". We wish him good luck.

Julian
No doubt I will be hanging up more washing and testing this fan/dehumidifier system to check it wasn't just a fluke. But, if that doesn't take up all my time, I will also be playing some Dorfromantik. I've had my eye on it for a while but after talking to the Volatiles devs about it's tile placing mechanic I was convinced to finally buy it.

And you, reader dear, what are you playing this weekend…?

items.title: Ambitious “Control Resonant” Challenges Expectations, Rewards Creativity
items.author: Brian Tallerico

items.text:
Even though people often love to point out this site’s namesake’s opinion on video games, since we began this coverage, we’ve tried to write about where the form intersects with film in cinematic franchises like “Silent Hill,” “Uncharted,” and “Resident Evil.” While playing the absolutely brilliant “Control Resonant,” I kept thinking of some of the most ambitious, game-changing science fiction films of all time, obvious influences like “The Matrix” and “Inception.”

But I also found myself pondering the work of David Lynch. How do “Twin Peaks” and Remedy Entertainment’s masterpiece intersect? It’s in a creator’s willingness to push boundaries, to use the visual language of dreams, and to find emotional grounding in the impossible. Creative Director Mikael Kasurinen has said via the review guide, “We wanted to make something that provokes. Something that feels like nothing you’ve played before.” Mission accomplished.

The excellent “Control” ended with hero Jesse Faden finding her brother Dylan, cleansing him of the infection by the all-powerful Hiss, and leaving him and the place known as The Oldest House under lockdown. Jesse became the Director of the FBC (Federal Bureau of Control) and promised to figure out a way to fix whatever had broken reality in New York City, allowing enemies from an extradimensional space to invade Gotham. Come to think of it: With its reality-shaking vision of Lovecraftian creatures that might literally be from Hell, “Control” has a bit of “Event Horizon” in its DNA, too.

Seven years after the Hiss invaded the Oldest House, Jesse wakes up Dylan and promptly disappears. Dylan becomes the hero of “Resonant,” which is one of many elements that give it a different aesthetic from its predecessor. One thing that takes a bit of getting used to is that this is not “Control 2” for a reason. It is a very different experience, trading the tight location work of the Oldest House for open-world gameplay with multiple zones and far more freedom of choice.

Early in “Resonant,” Dylan aligns with an FBC agent named Zoe de Vera, a companion who speaks to Dylan through the PS5 controller. You work with Zoe to figure out how an event called the “Patterning” has divided New York City from reality, leading to the invasion by thousands of creatures that want Dylan dead. As in many open-world games, you’re free to roam as Dylan, though the developers brilliantly layer in new powers for Faden that unlock new regions, combat approaches, and different enemies. The game balances wiping out packs of routine enemies, the occasional fight with a Resonant or boss, and alternating story and main missions.

The “Resonant” developers lean into significantly more RPG elements with Dylan than they did with Jesse. Skill trees, magical items, various weapons to choose for a loadout—it’s all deeply customizable. That said, combat works similarly no matter the angle you take. It’s mostly melee-based combat with a steady flow of strike-and-dodge mechanics, but you can also unlock special powers through game progress, including summoning allies to fight alongside you and hurling projectiles.

My first few hours with “Resonant” were mixed. It truly does require you to recalibrate expectations after the relatively linear first game. I found myself wandering New York City, unsure what to do and wondering why the story missions were kicking my ass. The answer is that this game doesn’t just encourage exploration; it requires it. You can’t push through only the story missions in “Resonant” because you won’t be strong enough. You need to complete side missions to level up and become strong enough to take on enemies like Resonants, but you also need to explore the city, wandering into places like laundromats and gyms to find upgrade resources.

After a couple of hours, “Resonant” kicks into gear and doesn’t look back. Several missions in this game rank among the best of the last several years, including one where you escape a sinkhole and one where Dylan plays with shadows of himself and a younger Jesse that are unquestionably moving. This game does things narratively that would terrify most writers’ rooms in games, TV, or film. The missions can be so wildly unpredictable—one minute you’re guiding a magical cat to fight a demon and the next you’re battling mold spore creatures that look like the kin of Bloaters from “The Last of Us.”

You can never quite tell where “Resonant” is going, which gives it the storytelling power of great film or television. It’s got enough authorial decisions through customization and exploration to make you feel like you’re in “Control,” but it also contains remarkably confident writing, not just in plot but dialogue and character work as well.

And then there’s the navigation. After a few clunky hours where even getting around NYC can feel tough, Dylan gains two powers: one that can pull him to points on buildings above him, and one that can basically turn the entire world on its axis. You know that scene in “Inception” wherein Elliot Page’s character flips the city on itself and they “walk up” a street?

Now imagine that in gameplay. While it sounds almost impossibly disorienting, the developers use it in just the right places, allowing Dylan to control not just through superpowered combat but by shifting the entire world around him. It leads to some of the most stunning level design in years, especially late in the game when the entire setting becomes pliable.

What Remedy Entertainment is doing with the “Alan Wake” and “Control” games is unlike anything else on the market. They’re accomplishing what so many great artists have done: Pushing back against the rules and expectations put on their form by so many years of conforming creators. We can argue all day about the definitions of art, but the ambition in “Control Resonant” is a sibling of what we so often look for in literature, film, or theatre, too. It’s that charge we all get when we can tell something is working in a way we haven’t really experienced before. Maybe more than any game this year, “Resonant” has it.

The Publisher provided a review copy of this title. It is now available on PS5, Xbox Series, and Windows.

The Sunday Papers is our weekly roundup of great writing about (mostly) videogames from across the web.

Sundays are for realising that this is speeder racing.
items.text:
The Sunday Papers is our weekly roundup of great writing about (mostly) videogames from across the web.

Sundays are for realising that this is speeder racing. No, not podracing. You're not skilled enough for that yet. You've got to get your reps in to be the best of the best on the tracks of the galaxy far, far away. You've got to beat Ary Quill, Griff Halloran, Soren Zaks, Katja Mox, and the rest. But it's futile. Because you won't beat one crocodile-shaped little creature. YOU WILL NEVER DEFEAT BIDDY BLAS. HE WILL BLAS PAST YOU IN A BLAS OF GLORY, BIDDYING YOU FAREWELL AS HE ROCKETS BY. HE IS THE GREATEST RACER WHO EVER LIVED. HE IS THE STAR WARS: GALACTIC RACER, AND THE FORCE SHINES OUT OF HIS BIDDY BOTTOM.

Oh, you're challenging him to a race? Prefer to be BIDDYLASTED INTO OBLIVION.

Right off the start, Biddy BIDDYLASTS his way into first place aboard his trusty speeder bike. You take off after him in your landspeeder. Your ramjet boost finally warms up as you zig-zag around looming rocks. You activate it. Immediately, a wall of text is shot into your eyeballs. You make out a name. Connor Makar. Then Eurogamer blue-tinged a vision of a Smashmouth video-worthy face.

Suddenly, there he was: a tiny man with bright red eyes and green hair, his gut looming over stumpy legs; a different sort of hero. I rolled up my sleeves and started to finesse: I made his jawline flat and angular, his mouth blobfish wide. I changed his hair to the most irregular option I could find, and giggled at my ridiculous, magnificent creation.

The burst of speed propels you a bit closer to Biddy just as the road snakes into a labyrinbthine cave complex. Seeing that he's in range, but scrabble for your ion bolt. It fires, but racer-seeking jolt of enery somehow misses as Biddy disappears over the edge of a jump. You realise too late that you're about to hit a mine he's dropped. As it rocks your craft, shards of words are flicked into your eyeballs. You make out the word Respec, and realise you've been inflicted with some Knowledge about the current state of games media.

"With Respec, we are lucky – we can take our time and slowly build that startup because its overheads are covered in the profit margins of a long-established, defensively budgeted business.

"But my worry is that a lot of great, talented people and institutional knowledge will be lost among those who don't have that option, who need a new job tomorrow."

You recover just in time to see Biddy scoot out of the caves and into a series of narrow hairpins. Pinning your afterburner boost, you try to get after him. Luckily, he struggles in the corner exits and your crisp drifting soon has you breathing down his neck again. You go to overtake using the short boost offered by your surge ability. Biddy and your are running side-by-side. He suddenly turns into your craft, side-swiping you towards a wall formed from the hull of a beached Star Destroyer. As you careen towards doom, you see more words scrawled on the sandblasted metal sheeting. One reads Unwinnable. Next to it is something about American Top 40 charts and monoculture.

Music is as fundamental a unifying force in the universe as gravity. There was real value, in my mind, to music fans listening to something like AT40. I understand that the music industry, like the entire friggin’ world, is completely different now, but I suspect that even the music that artists make has changed because of the individualized way we engage with it now. As we continue to drift apart as a society, the lack of a collective way to experience pop music is trivial in the grand scheme of things, but it feels significant when I’m driving at night, listening to the radio.

You recover before being dashed against the ruined ship and catch back up to Biddy. The finish line is in sight. You dig deep. Blas engages his ramjet. So do you. It's a drag race to the line. As you squeeze the boost ever harder, you look for inspiration to push you the few inches ahead that you'll need. You find it in some words from last week on the sudden death of Geordie wrestler Benjamin Satterley by Lewis Howse for Cultaholic.

I saw first-hand how seriously he took his craft after we had a match at the Neon Club in Jarrow in November of 2008. It wasn’t a great match, as the crowd was on the smaller and less responsive side, but it wasn’t a complete disaster or anything. Ben, however, was visibly upset by it afterwards, feeling we had a better match in us. I remember at the time wondering why he cared so much, since he’d be off to Japan or goodness knows where in no time at all, wrestling in front of thousands and on TV and pay-per-view.

Sam Worthington admitted in an interview that he showed up to the set of Wrath of the Titans completely out of shape to play a Greek demi-god, confessing that he should have communicated this to the director instead of surprising the crew on day one. On the other hand, Peter Jackson reflected at the Cannes Film Festival not too long ago on infamously replacing Ryan Gosling in his 2009 fantasy movie because the actor showed up on set, like Worthington, having gained weight without informing the production. Gosling was replaced by Mark Wahlberg, and he later told the story in an interview with The Hollywood Reporter. "We had a different idea of how the character should look. I really believed he should be 210 pounds... I just showed up on set, and I had gotten it wrong. Then I was fat and unemployed," he said.

The movie in question ended up being a disappointment; it underperformed at the box office and received poor reviews. Criticism was aimed, in particular, at Jackson's direction of the material. The movie was based on a book by Alice Sebold, and it's currently streaming in the United States on Peacock, but only for a little while longer. It also featured four-time Oscar nominee Saoirse Ronan in the lead role, along with a supporting cast that included Rachel Weisz, Stanley Tucci, and Susan Sarandon.

Collider Exclusive · 8 Questions · 2 Minutes
What Fantasy World Do You Belong To?
Middle-earth · Grand Line · The Continent · Camp Half-Blood

Pick your magic, your crew, where you want to wake up and who you would rather be fighting, and we will tell you which world you actually belong in. Four are open to you: an ancient kingdom living through its last good age, an endless sea full of pirates, a continent that pays people to kill monsters, and a summer camp where the Greek gods are extremely real and mostly a nuisance.

💍Middle-earth(Rings of Power)

👒Grand Line(One Piece)

🐺The Continent(The Witcher)

🔱Camp Half-Blood(Percy Jackson)

FIND YOUR WORLD →

01

What kind of power do you want?
Every one of these worlds runs on a completely different sort of magic.

ASomething ancient and half forgotten that came down through my family.
BSomething completely ridiculous that works in a fight and gets a laugh.
CNo magic at all, just training, potions and a very sharp sword.
DSomething I inherited from a parent I have barely met.

NEXT QUESTION →

02

Who is travelling with you?
Nobody gets through any of these stories entirely on their own.

AA fellowship drawn from every corner of the world who barely trust each other.
BA crew I picked up one at a time, all of whom would die for me.
CTwo or three people I would never describe out loud as friends.
DTwo mates from school who are exactly as out of their depth as I am.

NEXT QUESTION →

03

Where do you want to wake up tomorrow?
The best fantasy is usually just somewhere you would genuinely like to live.

AA high city of white stone with the sea somewhere far below.
BA ship under sail, with an island ahead that nobody has mapped.
CA rented room over a tavern, in a town I am leaving in the morning.
DA cabin at a summer camp with everybody else already awake outside.

NEXT QUESTION →

04

How are you making a living out there?
Even in fantasy somebody has to pay for the horse.

AI am not, because somebody far older than me decided this was my duty.
BTreasure, and I am not always careful about whose it used to be.
CI take contracts, since people will pay well for what they will not touch.
DI am fifteen and this is all technically a school trip.

NEXT QUESTION →

05

There is something in the woods. What do you do about it?
All four of these worlds keep something unpleasant out there in the dark.

ASend word to somebody who has seen this before, then hold the line.
BWalk straight in, because it is interesting and possibly edible.
CAsk what it has been eating and what the village is willing to pay.
DWork out which myth it escaped from, then improvise very badly.

NEXT QUESTION →

06

Who is the villain of your story?
The enemy tells you far more about a world than the hero ever does.

AAn ancient evil that has been patient for several thousand years.
BA government that has spent a long time calling itself the good guys.
CA man who turns out to be far worse than anything I hunt for money.
DA god, or possibly my own family, and quite likely both at once.

NEXT QUESTION →

07

What do you actually believe in out there?
Every world hands its heroes one rule and asks them to hold onto it.

ASome things are worth defending even when the odds are hopeless.
BNobody gets to tell me where I can go or what I am allowed to want.
CPick the lesser evil, and never pretend afterwards that it was not evil.
DMy friends come before anything a prophecy has to say about it.

NEXT QUESTION →

08

A thousand years from now, how are you remembered?
Eight questions in, this is the one that decides your world.

AIn a song, in a language hardly anybody still speaks.
BAs the one who got there first and proved the whole thing was possible.
CBarely, and mostly wrongly, in ballads I would absolutely hate.
DOn a plaque at a camp, read by kids about to do the same thing.

REVEAL MY WORLD →

The Map Is Drawn
Your World Is…

Four worlds and four completely different ideas of what a good life
looks like. This is where you belong, what it would ask of you, and what you would get back in
return.

The Rings of Power · Prime Video · Since 2022

Middle-earth

You belong somewhere old enough that the mountains have names and
somebody can still tell you who gave them. Middle-earth is for people who think the right
thing is worth doing even when it will not be finished in their lifetime.

This is the only world on the list where doing good is understood as a very long defeat,
fought anyway, by people who will never see how it ends.

You are drawn to grandeur, to white cities and deep forges and the sense that almost
everything you touch is older than your entire family line.

The Rings of Power is set in the last good age before it all goes wrong, which gives
every quiet scene in it a slightly unbearable weight.

You would take the hard road, and you would take it on foot.

One Piece · Manga since 1997 · Netflix 2023

The Grand Line

You want the sea, a crew, and absolutely nobody telling you where
you are allowed to go. The Grand Line is the world for people whose main ambition in life is
finding out what is over there.

One Piece has run for decades on one very simple engine, which is a group of people who
each want something impossible and have decided to go and get it together.

You collect people. Your ideal crew is a set of misfits who were each written off
somewhere else before you turned up and offered them a better idea.

The world is enormous and deliberately ridiculous, and the emotional gut punches land
harder because of that rather than in spite of it.

You would set sail knowing the map runs out, which is more or less the entire point of
it.

The Witcher · Netflix · Since 2019

The Continent

You would rather be feared and useful than liked and useless. The
Continent is a world where the monsters are the straightforward part of the job and the
people are where it all gets complicated.

Witchers get paid to do what nobody else will and resented for existing at all, which is
a trade most people would refuse and you would probably accept.

You have no real illusions about which side is the good one, largely because on the
Continent that question tends to have a disappointing answer.

The best of these stories are not about the fighting. They are about somebody with a
rigid code being repeatedly cornered into caring about people.

You would take the coin, finish the job properly, and be out of town before the story
got told wrong.

Percy Jackson · Disney+ · Since 2023

Camp Half-Blood

You want the myths to be real and loose in the actual world, and
you want to find out at about thirteen that you were never anywhere near as ordinary as
everybody kept telling you.

Percy Jackson takes the oldest stories we have and drops them into car parks and diners,
which makes the gods considerably funnier and a great deal worse.

You would be the kid every school gave up on, who turns out to have been built for
something nobody thought to test for.

The series is genuinely about friendship rather than destiny, and it says so out loud
every time a prophecy tries to get in the way.

Camp Half-Blood is the real fantasy here: a place where the thing that made you
difficult everywhere else is the thing that makes you belong.

We're talking, of course, about The Lovely Bones. A harrowing tale about a young girl's murder, the film was partially set in a fantastical limbo. Years later, another thematically similar film directed by Colin Trevorrow — The Book of Henry — would receive widespread ridicule. The Lovely Bones grossed around $93 million against a reported budget of $65 million, and it's now sitting at a 30% score on Rotten Tomatoes. The aggregator website's consensus reads, "It's stuffed full of Peter Jackson's typically dazzling imagery, but The Lovely Bones suffers from abrupt shifts between horrific violence and cloying sentimentality." The late critic Roger Ebert was particularly venomous in his review, calling The Lovely Bones "a deplorable film with this message: If you’re a 14-year-old girl who has been brutally raped and murdered by a serial killer, you have a lot to look forward to." You can watch the movie on Peacock and decide for yourself, but remember, it'll be removed from the platform on November 1. Stay tuned to Collider for more updates.

items.text:
Elijah Wood’s 12-Year-Old Dark Fantasy Classic Officially Becomes a Streaming Smash Hit

Image via Cartoon Network

Elijah Wood spent three movies helping save Middle-earth, but his career has given horror fans plenty to enjoy since he left the Shire. His turn in Maniac took him somewhere considerably nastier, while The Faculty remains an obvious pick for anyone planning an October movie marathon. Frodo might be his most recognizable role, but Wood has never needed a sword and a fellowship to hold an audience’s attention.

October also gives viewers an excuse to revisit the stranger corners of animation. A talking animal or a storybook setting can make a fantasy look inviting, right up until the characters discover what they’ve wandered into. For anyone whose Halloween rotation already includes Coraline and The Nightmare Before Christmas, there’s always room for another trip through a world where getting home is harder than it looks.

Now, Wood’s Over the Garden Wall has climbed into Prime Video's U.S. top 10 TV chart ahead of Halloween. According to FlixPatrol, the 2014 Cartoon Network miniseries jumped six places to number 9, landing just behind Lioness and above All American. Created by Patrick McHale, it follows brothers Wirt and Greg as they search for a way home through a mysterious forest. Its ten, approximately 11-minute episodes make the complete adventure an easy two-hour addition to an October watchlist.

Collider Exclusive · 8 Questions · 2 Minutes
What Fantasy World Do You Belong To?
Middle-earth · Grand Line · The Continent · Camp Half-Blood

Pick your magic, your crew, where you want to wake up and who you would rather be fighting, and we will tell you which world you actually belong in. Four are open to you: an ancient kingdom living through its last good age, an endless sea full of pirates, a continent that pays people to kill monsters, and a summer camp where the Greek gods are extremely real and mostly a nuisance.

💍Middle-earth(Rings of Power)

👒Grand Line(One Piece)

🐺The Continent(The Witcher)

🔱Camp Half-Blood(Percy Jackson)

FIND YOUR WORLD →

01

What kind of power do you want?
Every one of these worlds runs on a completely different sort of magic.

ASomething ancient and half forgotten that came down through my family.
BSomething completely ridiculous that works in a fight and gets a laugh.
CNo magic at all, just training, potions and a very sharp sword.
DSomething I inherited from a parent I have barely met.

NEXT QUESTION →

02

Who is travelling with you?
Nobody gets through any of these stories entirely on their own.

AA fellowship drawn from every corner of the world who barely trust each other.
BA crew I picked up one at a time, all of whom would die for me.
CTwo or three people I would never describe out loud as friends.
DTwo mates from school who are exactly as out of their depth as I am.

NEXT QUESTION →

03

Where do you want to wake up tomorrow?
The best fantasy is usually just somewhere you would genuinely like to live.

AA high city of white stone with the sea somewhere far below.
BA ship under sail, with an island ahead that nobody has mapped.
CA rented room over a tavern, in a town I am leaving in the morning.
DA cabin at a summer camp with everybody else already awake outside.

NEXT QUESTION →

04

How are you making a living out there?
Even in fantasy somebody has to pay for the horse.

AI am not, because somebody far older than me decided this was my duty.
BTreasure, and I am not always careful about whose it used to be.
CI take contracts, since people will pay well for what they will not touch.
DI am fifteen and this is all technically a school trip.

NEXT QUESTION →

05

There is something in the woods. What do you do about it?
All four of these worlds keep something unpleasant out there in the dark.

ASend word to somebody who has seen this before, then hold the line.
BWalk straight in, because it is interesting and possibly edible.
CAsk what it has been eating and what the village is willing to pay.
DWork out which myth it escaped from, then improvise very badly.

NEXT QUESTION →

06

Who is the villain of your story?
The enemy tells you far more about a world than the hero ever does.

AAn ancient evil that has been patient for several thousand years.
BA government that has spent a long time calling itself the good guys.
CA man who turns out to be far worse than anything I hunt for money.
DA god, or possibly my own family, and quite likely both at once.

NEXT QUESTION →

07

What do you actually believe in out there?
Every world hands its heroes one rule and asks them to hold onto it.

ASome things are worth defending even when the odds are hopeless.
BNobody gets to tell me where I can go or what I am allowed to want.
CPick the lesser evil, and never pretend afterwards that it was not evil.
DMy friends come before anything a prophecy has to say about it.

NEXT QUESTION →

08

A thousand years from now, how are you remembered?
Eight questions in, this is the one that decides your world.

AIn a song, in a language hardly anybody still speaks.
BAs the one who got there first and proved the whole thing was possible.
CBarely, and mostly wrongly, in ballads I would absolutely hate.
DOn a plaque at a camp, read by kids about to do the same thing.

REVEAL MY WORLD →

The Map Is Drawn
Your World Is…

Four worlds and four completely different ideas of what a good life
looks like. This is where you belong, what it would ask of you, and what you would get back in
return.

The Rings of Power · Prime Video · Since 2022

Middle-earth

You belong somewhere old enough that the mountains have names and
somebody can still tell you who gave them. Middle-earth is for people who think the right
thing is worth doing even when it will not be finished in their lifetime.

This is the only world on the list where doing good is understood as a very long defeat,
fought anyway, by people who will never see how it ends.

You are drawn to grandeur, to white cities and deep forges and the sense that almost
everything you touch is older than your entire family line.

The Rings of Power is set in the last good age before it all goes wrong, which gives
every quiet scene in it a slightly unbearable weight.

You would take the hard road, and you would take it on foot.

One Piece · Manga since 1997 · Netflix 2023

The Grand Line

You want the sea, a crew, and absolutely nobody telling you where
you are allowed to go. The Grand Line is the world for people whose main ambition in life is
finding out what is over there.

One Piece has run for decades on one very simple engine, which is a group of people who
each want something impossible and have decided to go and get it together.

You collect people. Your ideal crew is a set of misfits who were each written off
somewhere else before you turned up and offered them a better idea.

The world is enormous and deliberately ridiculous, and the emotional gut punches land
harder because of that rather than in spite of it.

You would set sail knowing the map runs out, which is more or less the entire point of
it.

The Witcher · Netflix · Since 2019

The Continent

You would rather be feared and useful than liked and useless. The
Continent is a world where the monsters are the straightforward part of the job and the
people are where it all gets complicated.

Witchers get paid to do what nobody else will and resented for existing at all, which is
a trade most people would refuse and you would probably accept.

You have no real illusions about which side is the good one, largely because on the
Continent that question tends to have a disappointing answer.

The best of these stories are not about the fighting. They are about somebody with a
rigid code being repeatedly cornered into caring about people.

You would take the coin, finish the job properly, and be out of town before the story
got told wrong.

Percy Jackson · Disney+ · Since 2023

Camp Half-Blood

You want the myths to be real and loose in the actual world, and
you want to find out at about thirteen that you were never anywhere near as ordinary as
everybody kept telling you.

Percy Jackson takes the oldest stories we have and drops them into car parks and diners,
which makes the gods considerably funnier and a great deal worse.

You would be the kid every school gave up on, who turns out to have been built for
something nobody thought to test for.

The series is genuinely about friendship rather than destiny, and it says so out loud
every time a prophecy tries to get in the way.

Camp Half-Blood is the real fantasy here: a place where the thing that made you
difficult everywhere else is the thing that makes you belong.

↻ RETAKE THE QUIZ

‘Over the Garden Wall’ Is a Halloween Binge You Can Finish in One Night

Image via Cartoon Network

Over the Garden Wall earns its Halloween appeal with a forest that looks inviting until you actually have to walk through it. The autumn scenery gives Wirt and Greg’s adventure a storybook charm, but the brothers never know whether their next encounter will help them get home or leave them in worse trouble. The show can be funny and genuinely unsettling within the same short episode, which makes watching “just one more” an easy trap to fall into.

Wood’s Wirt is an especially good guide through that uncertainty because he would clearly prefer to be almost anywhere else. Greg (voiced by Collin Dean), meanwhile, treats getting lost as another opportunity to have fun, often leaving his older brother to worry enough for both of them. Their back-and-forth banter keeps the series from becoming relentlessly grim, but it also gives the darker moments something to threaten. You want these two to get home, even if spending another episode in the woods sounds pretty tempting. The voice cast offers several other recognizable names, including Christopher Lloyd, John Cleese, and Chris Isaak. Their involvement gives newcomers something else to listen for, although Wood and Dean remain the central pairing.

With a new top-10 appearance ahead of Halloween, there’s a timely reason to take the trip, whether it’s your first visit or an annual return.

DFirst class, with a cover identity and a gadget that does something I won't explain until it's needed.

BCracks a one-liner, grabs a fire extinguisher or a chair, and improvises something that somehow works.

EA debrief that turns into three hours of contingency planning that somehow becomes the most fun you've had all week.

BDeadpan and dry — keeping it light keeps me sharp, even when everything is on fire.

ESomeone who steps forward instead of back — because that's who they've always been.

Your Partner Has Been Assigned
Your Perfect Partner Is…

Your answers have pointed to one action hero above all others. This is the person built to have your back — for better or considerably, spectacularly worse.

Rambo

Your partner doesn't talk much, doesn't need to, and will have assessed every threat in your immediate environment before you've finished your first sentence. John Rambo is not a man of plans or politics — he is a force of nature shaped by survival, loyalty, and a capacity for endurance that goes beyond anything training can produce. He will not leave you behind. He has never left anyone behind who deserved to come home. What you get with Rambo is the most capable, most quietly ferocious partner imaginable — one who has been through things that would have broken anyone else, and who chose to keep going anyway. You'll never need to ask if he has your back. You'll just know.

James Bond

Your partner will arrive perfectly dressed, perfectly briefed, and with a cover story so convincing it'll take you a moment to remember what's actually true. James Bond is the most professionally dangerous person in any room he enters — and the most disarmingly charming, which is the point. He operates in a world of layers, where nothing is what it appears and every advantage is used without apology. You'll never be bored. You'll occasionally be furious. But when it matters — when the mission is genuinely on the line and the margin for error has collapsed to nothing — Bond is exactly the partner you want. He has survived things that have no business being survivable. He does it with style. That is not nothing.

Indiana Jones

Your partner will know the history, the language, the cultural context, and exactly why the thing everyone else is ignoring is actually the most important thing in the room. Indiana Jones is brilliant, reckless, and occasionally impossible — but he is also one of the most resourceful, most genuinely knowledgeable partners you could find yourself beside. He approaches every situation with a scholar's eye and a brawler's instinct, which is an unusual combination and a remarkably effective one. He hates snakes and gets personally attached to objects of historical significance, both of which will slow you down at least once. It doesn't matter. What Indy brings is irreplaceable — and the adventures you'll have together will be the kind people write books about. Assuming you survive them.

John McClane

Your partner was not supposed to be here. He does not have the right equipment, the right information, or anything approaching the right odds. He has a sarcastic remark and an absolute refusal to accept that the situation is as bad as it looks. John McClane is the greatest accidental hero in the history of action cinema — a man whose superpower is stubbornness, whose contingency plan is improvisation, and whose capacity to absorb punishment and keep moving would be alarming if it weren't so useful. He will complain the entire time. He will make it significantly more chaotic than it needed to be. And he will absolutely, unconditionally, without question come through when it counts. Yippee-ki-yay.

Ethan Hunt

Your partner has already run seventeen scenarios by the time you've finished reading the briefing, and the plan he's settled on involves at least two things that should be physically impossible. Ethan Hunt operates at the absolute edge of human capability — technically, physically, and intellectually — and he brings the same relentless precision to protecting his partners that he brings to dismantling organisations that shouldn't exist. He is not easy to know and he will never fully tell you everything. But he will carry the weight of the mission so completely, so absolutely, that your job is simply to trust him — and the remarkable thing is that trusting him always turns out to be the right call. The mission will be impossible. He will complete it anyway.

Statham's movies tend to have long lives after leaving theaters anyway. Action thrillers are easy streaming viewing, and his back catalog regularly finds its way onto platform charts years after release.

Austin King is the Senior Editor of Gaming at ScreenRant and has been with the site since 2020 with a focus on RPGs and tabletop games. He previously managed content for Geek to Geek Media, and has served as a writer for sites like Nintendad, Geek Fitness, and more.
In addition to his work at ScreenRant, he also hosts the Dragon Quest FM podcast and is the author of several books, including co-writing Nimbus (a #1 bestseller in 2013). His latest is the nonfiction The Dragon Quest Book, available now.
He's written about pop culture, video games, and genre studies over the course of his career. You can find him on BlueSky, X, and at Dragonquestaustin.com

There are a lot of new The Lord of the Rings projects in the works right now. There's the new movies set in Peter Jackson's film trilogy universe, The Rings of Power show on Prime, some new video games in the works, and a successful tabletop RPG that will see new sourcebooks launching in 2027. And despite J.R.R. Tolkien's Middle-earth being about a century old, it's amazing that there's still new things to look forward to.

That list is about to grow even longer. One of the longest ongoing efforts from The Lord of the Rings franchise is about to release The Wolves of Mordor. On top of teasing hidden regions beyond Gorgoroth, The Wolves of Mordor will introduce a new threat into Tolkien's world of Middle-earth. And a new trailer has revealed just what to expect when The Wolves of Mordor arrives near the end of October.

The Wolves of Mordor trailer, which debuted on YouTube and can also be viewed above, shows off a number of things to expect with the new expansion arrives in The Lord of the Rings Online, the long-running MMORPG that's been adding new content since its debut in 2007. Among the many things the MMO is adding, the biggest might just be "were-wolves" that will stalk Mordor. These aren't upsized wolves or Wargs either, but a brand-new foe coming to Middle-earth.

The new update will also introduce Neighbours to its housing system, allowing companions to live in your home and form bonds with your character through daily tasks and gift-giving. There will also be 3 hidden new regions beyond the uncharted wilds of Draugardh: "the Mount Doom scorched Heledhris, the jagged plains of Parth Rhavas, and the shrouded forests of Nan Ogol." And of course, you'll also have those new were-wolf enemies to contend with as you explore the new zones.

The Wolves of Mordor is scheduled to launch on October 21, 2026, as part of The Lord of the Rings Online. In addition to the Standard Edition releasing for $39.99, there will also be a Collector's Edition for $79.99 and an Ultimate Edition for $129.99. The premium editions come with a host of extra in-game items, including Were-wolf Hunter cosmetics, a Hound pet, immediate access to Neighbours, and a 160 Were-wolf Hunter's level-up earring.
